Bibliography 104 3 Chapter 1 Introduction This project aims to leave the reader with an understanding of graph theory and how to apply its ideas to prove the four colour theorem. It begins with a consideration of the history behind the theorem, from when it was ﬁrst mentioned on record, to when it was ﬁrst proved some 200 years later. In order to grasp the ideas involved in this proof, we then cover aspects of graph theory. The four colour theorem is thus; a map can be coloured with no more than four colours in such a way that no two adjacent countries share a colour.Graph theory allows us to view these maps with a di↵erent structure, one involving only edges and vertices. In turn, this allows us to identify properties and study our maps with increased ease. While both of these begin as simple concepts, we will see that it results in a complex proof. On the surface one would be forgiven for not seeing the value in the four colour theorem. As we will see in Chapter 3, Leonhard Euler published a paper in 1736 which set out to solve the K¨onigsberg bridge problem [29], this brought about the beginnings of graph theory. Although the four colour theorem was ﬁrst noted 116 years later in 1852, it is considered to have vastly aided further development of graph theory [3, p.VII]. Real world advancements have resulted from this development of graph theory. For example, algorithms used in computer science are improving, and links to other areas of mathematics are beginning to surface and be useful [3, p.VIII]. Additionally, networking problems such as road networks, social media and even brain neuron connections can all be studied thanks to their shared properties with ideas from graph theory problems [34, p.3]. Indeed, the four colour theorem is not without its uses after all! 4 We have four main objectives in mind for this project. One is to explore the theorems’ history, and another is cover some graph theory concepts including corresponding examples and problems. We also want to cover colouring theorems, again with corresponding examples, and lastly we want to explore how to apply colouring ideas to di↵erent surfaces. To achieve this we will predominantly follow the ideas and deﬁnitions used in the Graph Theory book by J. A. Bondy and U. S. R. Murty [3]. 5 Chapter 2 History of the four colour theorem One puzzle that confounded mathematicians for nearly a century is the idea ‘that if an area be partitioned in any manner into areas, these can be, with four colours only, coloured in such wise that in every case two attached areas have distinct colours’ [6], or more commonly known as, the four colour theorem. Although some believe that this idea was originally observed by early cartographers, the ﬁrst known instance of it was in 1852 by a 21 year old mathematician called Francis Guthrie. Francis went on to attempt a proof, and told his brother Frederick Guthrie about the four colour conjecture, as it then was known. Frederick is known to have said that Francis’ proof ‘did not seem altogether satisfactory’ [28], however, he still passed on the conjecture to Augustus De Morgan, a well-renowned mathematician whom Frederick had become a student of. De Morgan then gave us the ﬁrst written record detailing the four colour theorem, when he wrote to fellow mathematician William Hamilton on the 23rd October 1852. In the letter, he queried if Hamilton could provide any insight into what Frederick had shown him, as he was at a loss to explain it. Hamilton sent a short reply on October 26th, ‘I am not likely to attempt your quaternion of colour very soon [23].’ De Morgan kept spreading awareness of the problem and a few mathematicians, such as Charles Pierce, did attempt to prove it. Despite an interest in the conjecture continuing, there was not much progress noted until 1878, when Arthur Cayley queried at a meeting of the London Mathematical 6 Society if a proof has been found. The lack of signiﬁcant progress reported spurred Cayley on to attempt it himself, and in 1879 he published On the Colouring of Maps [6]. In this paper, Cayley fails to ﬁnd a proof but does succeed in highlighting the di�culty found in solving the four colour conjecture. The paper begins with Cayley saying that it is easy to see that four colours are necessary, for example, if we had a circle split into three sectors and then we enclosed it, the enclosed space would need to be a fourth colour, see Figure 2.1. Additionally, if we had a circle split into four sectors, we again could colour it with four colours but three would su�ce. This showed Cayley, that in general, if the number of sectors is odd or even, then the number of colours required is four or three respectively. Going forward we will refer to any sector/space etc. as a country, and the collection of all these countries as a map. Think of a map of the United States of America, each state is known as a country and all ﬁfty of them make up the map. Figure 2.1: Cayley’s ﬁrst example - enclosed circles divided into three and four countries respectively. Cayley’s observation, however, does not provide a general proof, and gaining this is where the di�culty lies. To continue, he approaches the problem using mathematical induction. If we have n countries on a map, coloured as per the theorem with only four colours, and a (n +1)th country is added, we can not say that the new country can be successfully added without needing to alter the original colours ﬁrst. For example, see Figure 2.2 where the enclosing white represents the (n +1)th country. It is not possible to colour this country that encloses the pre-existing map, as all four colours are present in its interior boundary, i.e. the new country is connected to all four colours already. Therefore, we would have to change the circle and colour it with only 2 or 3 colours to be able to colour the (n +1)th country. 7 Figure 2.2: Cayley’s second example - an enclosed circle that results in a map that cannot be four coloured, unless we make alterations ﬁrst. Alternatively, Cayley shows that instead of enclosing a map with an additional county, it is possible to insert the new (n +1)th country into the map and obtain the same result. This is achieved by inserting it at a point where it will be adjacent to all four colours. This leaves us with the same conundrum that is being highlighted, a boundary containing all four colours that needs changing to make the conjecture succeed. This way of visualising the di�culty is how we will now proceed. Figure 2.3 shows us an example of this. We know the theorem states that it must be possible to colour the map, however we can see that it is not possible unless the colouring is altered. If we swap blue for red in one of the countries in the left hand side map, blue becomes available for the central country in the right. This works as we have changed the exterior boundary to only show three colours, though it could have been done with only two. Figure 2.3: Cayley’s third example - inserting a new country attached to each of the original countries. These observations led Cayley to add a condition to the conjecture; no more than three colours can be present in the external boundary. This condition is what makes it di�cult to prove. It would be insu�cient to provide a general proof without also showing that it only works if it is possible to have the boundary condition in place too. Despite this di�culty, Alfred Kempe on the 17th July 1879 announced that he had a proof. Kempe studied under Cayley, and it was per Cayley’s suggestion 8 that he submitted his proof to the American Journal of Mathematics. Before we can fully explore this proof, however, we need to introduce some graph theory concepts. These concepts will be expanded upon in more detail in Chapter 3. In graph theory, graphs are represented using edges, vertices and faces. Using our current analogy this translates to a graph being our map, the vertices (which can be coloured) being our countries, and the edges representing which countries are adjacent to one another. A face is an area that has been partitioned o↵ by these edges and vertices. To help visualise this, Figure 2.4 shows the second circle from Figure 2.3 represented this way. For example, we can see the blue vertex has edges connecting to each of the others, indicating that it is adjacent to them all, as it indeed is. Figure 2.4: Representation of a map in graph theory. In addition to this, we require the deﬁnition of a planar graph.This is a graph that can be drawn in the above way, without any lines crossing over. If the maximum number of edges are used in such a graph, meaning to add any more would make it nonplanar, then it is called maximal planar. Figure 2.5: This is known as the pentatope graph. We can see that if we try drawing it without edges crossing that we fail, and therefore this is not a planar graph. These deﬁnitions are important as Kempe recognised that the type of graph needed for the four colour conjecture is planar, and he combined this with Euler’s Formula to prove that a planar graph ‘must contain at least one country that is adjacent to ﬁve or fewer other countries [28].’ 9 On a side note, Leonhard Euler was a prominent mathematician, who in 1736 wrote the ﬁrst paper using graph theory [3, p.86], and we will be seeing more ideas from his work. The number of edges connecting to a vertex is that vertex’s degree,and here represents how many countries it is adjacent to. So Kempe’s above idea in other words is, if a graph has all vertices ‘degree 6 or higher, then the graph would not be planar [5].’ This means that for Kempe’s proof, he only had to show that it is possible to colour maps for cases that contain countries that are adjacent to ﬁve or fewer other countries. Kempe’s proof was presented in an article with few visual examples and limited mathematical notation, so we will consider [28] which provides a more modern insight to Kempe’s method. The proof we have just derived means that proof for the four colour conjecture needs only be found for cases when ﬁve or less countries border another. 11 To start with we have the base step; a map with four or less countries can be coloured using no more than four colours. Now we assume that this holds true for all maps with n countries, and let M be a map with n +1 countries. We know that M must contain at least one country that is adjacent to ﬁve or fewer countries. Letting this country be known as X,we then build the map M � X with the countries arranged in such a way that if we extended their boundaries into the excluded X they would meet at a point. See Figure 2.7. Figure 2.7: A map showing the Czech Republic as our X country, the lighter colours highlighting how the other countries could be extended to meet at one point. Kempe’s aim is to now reduce the number of colours used in the countries surrounding X, so that a colour is available for X.We can see for cases where X is surrounded by three or less countries that X can already be coloured. For cases with four or ﬁve surrounding countries, made up from three or less colours, again we can see X can already be satisﬁed. It remains that we need to consider cases where X is adjacent to four countries with four di↵erent colours, like in Figure 2.7, and cases where X is adjacent to exactly ﬁve countries coloured with four colours, like in Figure 2.8. Figure 2.8: A map showing Slovakia as the X country, this time surrounded by ﬁve countries representing four colours. To make his proof Kempe introduced a method called Kempe chains.A Kempe chain is a region made up from two continuously connected colours, for example in Figure 2.8 we have a red-yellow chain going from 12 Belgium-France-Italy-Austria. To state Kempe’s argument simply, to make a map colourable you just need to interchange the colours in one or two chains that end in the boundary of X. Case 1. X is adjacent to four countries. Case 1 is split into two parts, the ﬁrst being when non-adjacent regions in the boundary of X belong to di↵erent chains of the same colours. Figure 2.9: Case 1: Part 1. We have separate yellow-green chains coming from Germany A and Slovakia C,interchanging the colours in the Germany chain has meant X could be successfully coloured yellow. Part 2 of Case 1 considers if the opposing sides belong to the same chain. In this instance, say we had a red-yellow chain, as the chain loops from one country to the other it would enclose countries that are in a blue-green chain preventing them from contacting the other blue-green chain that stems from the boundary. So to open up a colour for X,the colours in one of the blue-green chains would need inverting. See Figure 2.10. Figure 2.10: Case 1: Part 2. This time Germany A and Slovakia C share the same yellow-green chain, so interchanging their colours would not help. The chain has looped around Switzerland and Austria’s D blue-red chain, thereby separating it from Poland’s B chain. So we can invert a blue-red chain to get a successful colouring for X. 13 Case 2. X is adjacent to ﬁve countries. Again, this case is split into two parts. Firstly, if we consider how the ﬁve countries are coloured, we can see that there will always be one country sandwiched between the same colour. Let the countries with the same colour be A and B,thecolourinthemiddle be C,and the othertwobe D and E. Then part 1 of this case is when, C belongs to a di↵erent, but same coloured, chain as D or E.In this instance, like in Case 1: Part 1, we interchange the colours in one of the chains. See Figure 2.11. Figure 2.11: Case 2: Part 1. Here we have C being Austria, and its red-green chain is separate to the red-green chain of the Ukraine D.Therefore, interchanging one of these chains will free up a colour for X. In this example, C also has a separate red-yellow to Poland’s red-yellow chain but that could have been connected, we just need one of D or E’s chains to not be connected to C’s. The ﬁnal part to Kempe’s proof is the case when C belongs to the same chain as D and the same chain as E.In this scenario, the two chains keep countries A and B apart, and to free up a colour for X we need to invert both of their colours. See Figure 2.12. Figure 2.12: Case 2: Part 2. Here the Ukraine is the C country in the middle of A and B.It shares a red-yellow chain with D, the Czech Republic, and a red-green chain with E, Austria. This leaves us the green-blue chain of A and the blue-yellow chain of B segregated from one another. B,although it does not in this example have a yellow in the chain, is considered as blue-yellow as yellow is the colour it is not adjacent to from the boundary. Inverting A and B frees up the blue for X. 14 This concludes Kempe’s proof from 1879, and for the eleven years following it, the four colour conjecture became the four colour theorem. Kempe received critical acclaim for his proof, and was elected as a fellow of the Royal Society in 1881, going on to be its treasurer and vice-president [23]. The error in Kempe’s proof is not obvious. The fault is found in Case 2: Part 2, and it was Percy Heawood, a British mathematician, who produced a counterexample in 1890. In Heawood’s paper he states, ‘The present article does not profess to give a proof of this original Theorem; in fact its aims are so far rather destructive’ [17]. His proof was simply evidence that Kempe had failed to observe a third option within Case 2. Case 2 being that after ﬁnding chains from C to D and C to E,we invert the chains leading from A and B. However, Heawood found that it is possible that the chains from A and B might share a boundary, and this touching of the chains would mean that inverting them both would not be beneﬁcial. At the point that they touch, if those two chains were inverted, we would have two adjacent countries that are both the original colour of A and B, and so not satisfying the four colour conjecture. Figure 2.13: Heawood’s original sketch which disproved Kempe’s theorem [17]. Translating Figure 2.13 into the terms we have been considering, we have the X country in the center without a colour assigned to it. Then the C country is the blue one bordering X as it is sandwiched between two reds, representing A and B.Then we can see that C connects in a blue-yellow chain to the yellow D, and with a blue-green chain to the green E.This leaves, A (the red higher up) a red-green chain, and B and red-yellow chain. These two chains touch on the right hand side of the ﬁgure, where green and yellow are adjacent. If, as per Kempe’s proof, we inverted both A and B’s chains, these touching countries would both become red, and so would not satisfy the theorem, and so it has been disproved. 15 Figure 2.14: Example 2: The star denotes the point where the chains from A and B touch, and show how inverting them does not work for this case. Heawood, unlike Kempe, did not receive any honour for his contribution, and in future discussions of Kempe’s proof his ﬁndings were hard to ﬁnd a record of, with some still believing that the proof stood strong [2]. Despite this, today Heawood is credited with the discovery as well as ﬁnding the ﬁrst proof of the 5 colour theorem, which we will discover later. Kempe himself had reported the error to the London Mathematical Society, saying that he could not solve this ‘case of failure [28].’ Kempe’s proof would remain the best attempt for almost a century. In 1904 a new graph theory concept, unavoidable sets,was being widely studied. In 1922, Philip Franklin, an American mathematician, published work that used unavoidable sets, along with other ideas, to prove that any map M is four colourable with  25 countries. As more people got involved with the concept, the number increased. In 1926 it was proved for  27 countries, in 1940 for  35 countries, in 1970 for  39 and in early 1976 for  95 countries [23]. The next full proof came in 1976 from Kennet Appel & Wolfgang Haken. This proof renamed the four colour conjecture back into the four colour theorem for the last time, due to it remaining a successful and validated theorem. This ﬁnal proof expanded upon work started by Heinrich Heesch, a German mathematician. Heesch, during the 1960’s and 70’s, had begun to develop modern computer based proof methods. He used his own method of discharging for the four colour theorem, discussed in later chapters, and it was this that set vital groundwork for Appel & Haken to complete the proof [23]. Unfortunately for Heesch, he could not secure the supercomputer time needed to solve it himself. Appel & Haken used the idea of unavoidable sets, the method of discharging, and methods of reducibility using Kempe chains, to check over 1400 cases on 16 a computer. This was the ﬁrst theorem proof ever found via computer, as this made it di�cult to verify the results by hand it was met with some scepticism. However, as other veriﬁcation came about supporting Appel & Haken, the proof became more and more accepted. In 1997, four mathematicians, Robertson, Sanders, Seymour & Thomas, published a report which improves on Appel & Haken’s algorithm so that less cases need to be considered. They clearly explain the concern few have about computer use in their conclusion, ‘our “proof” is not a proof in the traditional sense, because it contains steps that can never be veriﬁed by humans...These have to be taken on faith, and are conceivably a source of error [27].’ In 2005, Georges Gontier wrote his Formal Proof—The Four-Color Theorem report. In this, he outlines his use of the Coq programming language to formalise his version of the proof [14]. This lessens the worry about computer usage as the Coq proof assistance checks the proof process itself not just the mathematics being applied, meaning only the programming language has to be trusted to not create computational errors. New ideas will be introduced to help develop an understanding of the mathematics needed to solve the ﬁnal proof, in order to satisfy the objectives of this report. 17 Chapter 3 Graph theory In Chapter 2, we have already introduced some graph theory concepts. This chapter aims to formalise those and introduce more, until we have laid out enough groundwork to discuss the four colour theorem in Chapter 4. Graph theory was ﬁrst seen in a paper written by Swiss mathematician Leonhard Euler, called the Solutio problematis ad geometriam situs pertinentis, which he wrote in Latin. Published in 1736, this fourteen page paper sets about solving the K¨onigsberg bridge problem [29]. K¨onigsberg at the time of Euler’s publication was part of Prussia, and today it is a small city called Kaliningrad in Russia. The city is split by a river that contains a loop, e↵ectively splitting the city into four parts, and seven bridges were built to allow access to all districts. Figure 3.1: Euler’s original sketch, showing the locations of the seven bridges [11]. The problem was thus; is it possible to take a walk around the city, while only crossing each bridge once? Initially Euler was hesitant to attempt the problem, saying in a letter to the mayor of Danzig in Poland, ‘this type of solution bears little relationship to mathematics, and I do not understand why you expect a mathematician to produce it’ [24]. However, after considering the problem and concluding that it was not so trivial after all, Euler said, to an Italian mathematician called Giovanni Marinoni, it ‘seemed to me worthy of attention in that [neither] geometry, nor algebra, nor even the art of counting 18 was su�cient to solve it [24].’ Having to utilise new methods brought about the beginnings of graph theory. We can see in Figure 3.1 that Euler labeled each distinct area A, B, C and D. Additionally, he said that the connection from A to B via the crossing of a bridge could be denoted (A, B). This idea is the birth of vertices and edges in graph theory. 3.1 Graph theory basics Firstly, we need to note that we are going to consider graphs of a ﬁnite nature, though inﬁnite graphs do exist, as we will discover soon.
